claim: Yang et al. propose VIA-SPiRL, a contact-rich manipulation learner that encodes 200 finite-state-machine demonstrations per peg shape into a latent skill prior and lets a Soft Actor-Critic policy choose both latent motion skills and Cartesian stiffness. On a Franka robot, the method is reported to learn circular, square, and triangular peg insertion within 100 online episodes per shape and to outperform direct SAC, behavior-cloning-plus-SAC, PILCO, fixed-impedance SPiRL, and the demonstration controller under the tested offsets. Its safety advantage is empirical: the skill prior and learned reduction of stiffness during contact avoided emergency stops in the reported VIA-SPiRL trials, whereas direct variable-impedance SAC and some fixed-stiffness trials triggered stops. There is no proof of policy convergence, passivity, collision avoidance, or force-bound satisfaction, and transfer deteriorates when the target geometry is not represented by the demonstrations.
claim_locator: Section IV, Variable Impedance Skill Learning
Section V-D, Adaptation to Different Shapes
epistemic_status: qualified: the architecture, demonstration source, hardware protocol, success rates, and emergency-stop observations are directly reported; optimization convergence and interaction safety are not analytically guaranteed, and generalization evidence is confined to three insertion geometries and tested pose offsets
problem_and_setting: The paper addresses direct reinforcement learning of motion and impedance for contact-rich manipulation, where unrestricted exploration can generate collisions and where a single fixed stiffness is inadequate across free motion, contact search, and insertion. The physical setting is a Franka Emika Panda performing circular, square, and triangular peg insertion. The policy observes joint position and velocity, position offset, end-effector rotation about z, and measured contact force, and selects a latent motion skill together with translational and z-axis rotational stiffness.
method_or_mechanism: VIA-SPiRL extends the SPiRL skill-prior framework with variable impedance. For each shape, 200 suboptimal demonstration trajectories are generated by a hand-coded finite-state machine using spiral search and phase-specific fixed stiffness. An LSTM variational autoencoder learns short-horizon latent skills and a learned prior predicts likely skills from state. During online learning, a SAC-style high-level policy selects a latent skill and four stiffness components; the decoder emits pose increments while a low-level Cartesian impedance controller executes the pose and gains. The action contains three translational stiffnesses and one z-axis rotational stiffness; other rotational coordinates are omitted, null-space stiffness is fixed, and damping is deterministically tied to stiffness by a critical-damping heuristic. Action normalization prevents the stiffness scale from dominating latent actions.
content_summary: The authors train directly on a Franka at 5 Hz for up to 100 episodes of 300 high-level actions, corresponding to about two hours and 30,000 online transitions per shape, with three training seeds. VIA-SPiRL is compared with direct SAC, BC+SAC, PILCO, fixed-impedance SPiRL, and the original finite-state-machine demonstrations. The reported learning curves show VIA-SPiRL alone learning all three shapes within the episode budget; direct SAC with variable impedance readily collides and can invoke robot braking. In 100-trial evaluations at several initial offsets and rotations, success generally falls as displacement grows; at 5 cm offset the reported success rates are 0.77, 0.68, and 0.60 for circular, square, and triangular pegs. Learned policies commonly lower stiffness upon contact and raise task-relevant stiffness during insertion. Cross-shape adaptation uses 50 additional episodes and ten trials per condition: square- or triangular-trained agents adapt well to the circular peg, but circular-trained agents transfer poorly to noncircular shapes. The authors attribute this asymmetry to dynamics absent from the source demonstrations.
synthesis_role: Provides physical-robot evidence that demonstration-conditioned latent skills can make online variable-impedance reinforcement learning more data efficient and less collision-prone than direct exploration in a narrow insertion family. It supports skill priors as an empirical exploration bias, not as a certified stability or safety layer.
development_link: Relative to fixed-impedance SPiRL, VIA-SPiRL makes stiffness part of the learned high-level action and exposes a compliance-performance trade-off during contact. Relative to direct SAC, the demonstration-derived latent prior constrains exploration toward previously observed motion structure. Relative to analytical adaptive or passive impedance controllers, the method learns task behavior from trials but supplies no Lyapunov, passivity, or force-constraint result. Its transfer experiment also shows that a skill prior can hinder or fail to help when demonstrations omit the contact dynamics of a new geometry.

evidence.locator: Section IV, network and action formulation
evidence.finding: A demonstration-trained LSTM skill encoder/decoder and state-conditioned prior are combined with a SAC-style policy that selects a latent motion skill plus three translational and one rotational stiffness values; damping is tied to stiffness and null-space stiffness remains fixed.

Experiments use a Franka robot, 200 finite-state-machine demonstrations per peg shape, three training seeds, 100 episodes per shape, 300 actions per episode at 5 Hz, and approximately two hours of online robot training.

evidence.locator: Section V-B, learning curves and baseline discussion
evidence.finding: VIA-SPiRL is reported to learn all three insertion tasks within the budget; direct variable-impedance SAC easily causes collisions and emergency braking, while other baselines fail or learn less reliably.

Across 100 trials per tested offset/rotation condition, success decreases at larger displacements; at 5 cm offset the paper reports success of 0.77 for circular, 0.68 for square, and 0.60 for triangular insertion.

evidence.locator: Section V-C, stiffness and force plots
evidence.finding: The learned policy lowers stiffness when contact is detected and adjusts task-relevant axes during insertion; high fixed stiffness exceeds the paper's 30 N force threshold, and two triangular fixed-stiffness trials cause emergency stops.

After 50 additional episodes, policies trained on square or triangular insertion adapt more successfully to a circular peg than a circular-trained policy adapts to the two noncircular pegs; the authors link the failure to unrepresented interaction dynamics.

evidence.locator: Section VI and absence of a stability section
evidence.finding: The paper supplies empirical learning and robot results but no theorem establishing policy convergence, passivity, closed-loop stability under time-varying gains, collision avoidance, or satisfaction of the 30 N threshold.

boundary_conditions: Evidence is limited to one Franka robot and three peg-in-hole geometries using closely related spiral-search insertion structure.

The 600 total demonstration trajectories are generated by a hand-coded finite-state machine rather than diverse human demonstrations, so the learned prior inherits that controller's state-action coverage and biases.

The impedance action is restricted to diagonal stiffness in translation and rotation about z; other rotational axes are ignored, null-space stiffness is fixed, inertia is fixed, and damping is not learned independently.
Training is performed directly on hardware for only three seeds, and the paper does not report inferential statistics supporting broad cross-method claims.
Success deteriorates as initial displacement increases, with the triangular peg remaining the hardest tested geometry.
The 30 N value is an experimental force threshold near the robot's braking behavior, not a formally enforced constraint.
Cross-shape evaluation uses only ten trials per adaptation condition and 50 additional episodes, and it does not establish zero-shot generalization.
No formal stability, passivity, safe-exploration, or collision-avoidance property covers the learned time-varying impedance policy.
assumptions: The finite-state-machine demonstrations cover motion skills and contact regimes relevant enough for the online task and new initial conditions.
The latent decoder continues to generate physically useful short-horizon pose increments when the high-level policy departs from demonstrated state distributions.
Measured force and pose-offset observations are sufficiently accurate and timely for contact-sensitive stiffness adaptation.
The low-level Cartesian impedance controller realizes the commanded diagonal stiffness and tied damping without destabilizing unmodeled contact dynamics.
Critical-damping selection from stiffness is adequate despite fixed inertia and incomplete rotational impedance adaptation.
Emergency-stop frequency and the measured-force threshold are meaningful empirical safety proxies for the tested setup.

reported: Direct SAC with variable impedance easily produces collisions and can activate emergency braking during real-robot learning.
Fixed high stiffness can exceed the 30 N force threshold, and two triangular fixed-stiffness trials trigger emergency stops.
Success decreases for larger initial position offsets, especially for the triangular peg.

A policy learned for one shape cannot be directly applied reliably to another; circular-to-square and circular-to-triangular adaptation is inferior because relevant dynamics are absent from the source demonstrations.
PILCO and the other learning baselines do not learn all three tasks within the reported real-robot budget.
inferred: The skill prior reduces dangerous exploration only when the demonstration distribution contains safe and task-relevant behavior; out-of-distribution contacts may still produce unsafe gains or motions.
Because the controller has no energy or passivity constraint, rapid learned stiffness changes can inject energy even when observed trials remain stable.
The four-dimensional diagonal stiffness action cannot express coupled or full six-dimensional compliance needed in more general contact-rich manipulation.
Training success over three seeds and a narrow task set does not establish algorithmic convergence or robust sample-efficiency across robots and contact conditions.
Emergency-stop avoidance in reported VIA-SPiRL trials should not be interpreted as certified safety or a guaranteed force limit.
